articles.title: ‘I hope this email finds you’: Microsoft declares outage over as the world digs out of its inbox
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Steven Sinofsky was relieved this week to finally give up a title he never wanted.

“Somewhat happy to say I am no longer responsible for the worst Outlook outage,” the former Microsoft executive posted on X Friday, sharing a May 2000 news story about the “I Love You” worm, which overwhelmed corporate email systems when he ran the Office group.

Later in the day, he aired a pet peeve. After a plumber emailed to say he’d missed an appointment because of the “Outlook outage,” Sinofsky noted that this one wasn’t really the application’s fault. “This time it is the data center layer,” he wrote .

Microsoft’s explanation backs him up. The company says the failure, which cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries this week, was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade in its Microsoft 365 cloud and surfaced after a more recent network change. It hasn’t given more details.

The company said late Friday it had restored service to the remaining customers and regions. The disruption lasted about 30 hours, according to Microsoft’s incident log . Microsoft offered a public apology and promised a detailed post-mortem explaining what went wrong and next steps.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, said on X Friday afternoon that “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” made recovery more difficult than normal.

A “thundering herd” isn’t a stampede of frustrated IT admins descending on Redmond, as fitting as that might have been. It happens when huge numbers of devices try to reconnect at the same time, overwhelming systems as they come back online.

He said the post-mortem would come “shortly,” with a “step-by-step timeline and our many repair items to avoid similar outages in the future.” In a reply to another user , he said Microsoft “will be very specific on what happened.” In its notice to customers, Microsoft said it would provide a preliminary post-incident report within two business days and a final report within five.
In the meantime, like prior incidents involving AWS and others, the “Outlook outage” became the latest example of how much depends on one company’s cloud.
Microsoft reported in January that it had more than 450 million paid commercial Microsoft 365 seats, roughly one for every 18 people on Earth.

Among those affected this week were Unity Health Toronto , a hospital network that had to declare a Code Grey, the alert for a systems failure; a Colorado jail that couldn’t take online bond payments ; and Pennsylvania lawmakers who went about 18 hours without email. Unity Health said patient care continued without disruption.
In Japan, securities firms and asset managers fell back on fax machines when trade-confirmation emails stopped coming through, Business Upturn reported , citing Nikkei.

In New York, the city’s Emergency Management office warned of delays reaching city agencies. In Singapore, the outage disrupted some government systems , including email, and in London, the UK Supreme Court wasn’t receiving email.

About the only thing that wasn’t Microsoft’s fault was Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop. Federal officials blamed aging FAA telecom gear . Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened an evening news conference — before even getting to the news that U.S. airspace had reopened — by saying there was “no connection between this and Microsoft,” adding, “I know a lot of people are making that jump.”
Microsoft itself looked to preempt the speculation a few hours earlier, posting on X that it had “no indication that the FAA’s nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services.”

The Microsoft 365 outage was at least the fourth significant one this year. A January outage lasted nearly 10 hours , and in July a bug in Microsoft’s automated network maintenance system disrupted Azure and Microsoft 365 services for hours. On Aug. 31, an Exchange Online outage also hit Teams, OneDrive and SharePoint.

Instead of “I hope this email finds you well,” many people joked , it should just be “I hope this email finds you.” (Consider this our nomination for the “Overworked Twitter Joke of the Week” on The Ringer’s Press Box podcast .)

Microsoft said Friday afternoon that it was watching the backlog of delayed email “to ensure all process successfully before considering the issue resolved.” The University of Washington’s IT department told its users that email delayed during the outage would be delivered as mail queues continued to be processed.
Many people coped with the flood of returning email with a bit of levity.

As the mail started flowing again, CNN chief media analyst Brian Stelter said he was getting “a deluge of emails from PR people pitching their clients to talk about the Outlook outage.” Most were sent during the outage, he noted, “which, fittingly, prevented the pitches from reaching me.”
The security company Malwarebytes captured the paradox in a message to its followers: “We regret to inform you that Teams and Outlook are coming back online after a global outage.”

articles.title: Gov. Ferguson seeks $10M to help develop Eastern Wash. clean-energy hub
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Gov. Bob Ferguson is proposing $10 million to fund basic infrastructure needed for the Northwest Advanced Clean Energy Park, a master-planned industrial area in Eastern Washington that will foster development of large-scale clean energy, advanced manufacturing and supply chains. The proposal will be included in his 2027–29 capital budget.
If approved by lawmakers, the funding would support sewer, water, electrical and road infrastructure at the park.
“This investment will support thousands of good-paying jobs in the trades and advanced industries, and unlock billions in private investment,” Ferguson said in a statement.

The 1,641-acre site was formerly part of the Hanford Nuclear Reservation, a sprawling federal property along the Columbia River near the Tri-Cities that is undergoing a massive environmental cleanup. Hanford was established during World War II to produce plutonium for the Manhattan Project.

According to the governor’s office, two projects have committed to locating at the park once infrastructure construction is complete: Atlas Agro’s low-carbon fertilizer production plant and the utility-scale Ruby Flats Solar Farm.

State officials said General Matter is also considering the location for producing advanced nuclear fuel for small reactors. That siting could potentially be beneficial for another project planned for the same area: Amazon, X-energy and Energy Northwest are developing plans for the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility , a nuclear plant comprised of clustered, small reactors.

In 2024, the Norwegian company Cenate expressed interest in building a factory at the park to produce lithium-ion battery components, according to the Tri-Cities Area Journal of Business , ultimately withdrew its plans.

The Tri-Cities is also attracting fusion-energy investment. Last year, Seattle startup Avalanche Energy landed a $10 million grant from the Washington State Department of Commerce’s Green Jobs Grant Program to develop FusionWERX, a commercial-scale testing facility for fusion technologies. The project is being developed in an existing Port of Benton building in Richland.
Washington is heading into its 2027–29 biennial budget with a multibillion-dollar shortfall , but officials have not yet settled on a definitive public estimate.

Ferguson has acknowledged the scale of the gap but has not publicly specified an amount. The shortfall concerns the state’s operating budget, which is separate from the capital budget funding proposed for the energy park.

articles.title: Alternative Transit Modes
articles.author: Martin Pagel
paras: As I explained in an earlier guideway post, Sound Transit chose light rail technology to make it easier to use the existing transit tunnel and to run and stop at grade but many new technologies have been developed since. As Sound Transit builds a lot more elevated and tunneled sections and opens new lines in urban areas, it may need to reevaluate that decision. Sound Transit and Metro already use buses, heavy rail (for Sounder), ferries, and trams. Other cities like San Francisco, Mexico, and Paris use even more different modes like people movers and gondolas. In that post I talked about monorail and maglev guiderail systems. They are easier and faster to build due to prefabricated guideways, are slicker and therefore visually less obtrusive, and may offer easier maintenance.

As Sound Transit is facing escalating construction costs and feels it cannot accommodate traditional elevated trains downtown, it may be a good time to evaluate these and other alternative transit modes. Monorail systems have opened in Bangkok, and TSB has built a maglev test line in China and is looking at several options in Germany. Swyft Cities (working with Whoosh Solutions) and Ottobahn are working on cabins which hang from a guideway like the Wuppertaler Schwebebahn and provide personal rapid transit (PRT).

Similar to a Waymo or Zoox robotaxi, Swyft Cities and Ottobahn offer more route flexibility, are called via phone app, and have small individual cabins with an electric motor. Unlike a robotaxi, they use airspace and don’t get stuck in traffic, they are confined to its track network, have specific parking/staging areas, use electric motors with track power, and use small stations. While Swyft cabins travel on fixed cables (similar to a gondola or the RopeTaxi but those are propelled by the cable), Ottobahn cabins travel on regular tracks at 37mph. For longer distances Ottobahn claims up to 150mph. Both use track switches to guide cabins to their destination.

Ottobahn cabins hang off a bogie which is powered by an electric motor with regular wheels and steel tracks. Cabins either stop at elevated stations or can employ a lift mechanism which drops the cabin to the sidewalk for on- and off-boarding. Ottobahn claims they can support 6000 riders per hour in each direction, or even more with a favorable network design. Similar to a monorail, their track is supported by towers about 120ft apart and between 15 and 30ft high. The track can also cross longer distances over rivers and other obstacles akin to a suspension bridge. Cabins can usually climb up to 7%, with extra support even 12%. That may allow a ship canal crossing.
Swyft is hoping to start projects in Queenstown, Miami, or Los Angeles. Ottobahn started construction of its first network in Phuket .

Traditional train lines serve stations along a linear corridor. Turning a train around at the end of the line takes time as the operator usually has to switch from one end of the train to the other. Lines may branch towards the outer area of a network, but that splits the headway on each branch. As automated train systems do not need to worry about a driver, they can switch direction more easily and offer a bit more flexibility. For example, they can serve short stub lines by backing in and out, though that may impact travel time. PRT systems are not bound to any fixed line/schedule, can use a more elaborate track network, branch on demand, skip stations, and only stop as necessary. Though each cabin may be smaller, short headways may still allow for sufficient capacity.

Any of these systems promise simpler/faster guideway and station construction, easier integration into the existing urban infrastructure, more flexible branching capabilities, and more convenience for riders. It may be worthwhile to consider them for West Seattle or Ballard and other future lines.

articles.title: Seattle Street Ends: Eastlake
articles.author: John Feit (Guest Contributor)
paras: Today we will visit eight street ends and one park in the Eastlake neighborhood. In previous posts, we have looked at street ends around West Seattle , South Ship Canal , from Ballard to Fremont , from Fremont to Portage Bay , as well as the Duwamish Waterway . The last post was for South Lake Union's street ends .

For those new to this series, a little background on Seattle’s Shoreline Street Ends is helpful. Because Seattle is bounded and divided by numerous fresh and salt bodies of water the city has what are called ‘street ends’ — streets that end when they encounter a water body often continue under the water, sometimes resulting in mini-parks or recreational spaces. There are hundreds of such occurrences – almost as many as there are east-west and north-south streets.
Many of them, 142 to be exact, are part of a Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) program called Shoreline Street Ends. The program’s goals are to:

A little over half of the 142 street ends are defined by SDOT as “worth a visit,” while the remainder are either “not yet ready for visitors” or have “no public access.” Street ends are concentrated along the Ship Canal and Lake Washington, but also occur along each of the city’s other shorelines. Working with the city and neighborhoods to secure funding, pass legislation, and organize work parties, the non-profit and all-volunteer Friends of Street Ends help ensure Seattle’s accessible street ends grow in number and those already serving visitors continue to thrive.

Shoreline Street Ends vary in character from sandy beaches to docks wedged amongst shipyards and industrial uses. They are spacious and they are compact, and most are very easy to find. They support habitat for native species of flora and fauna and are convenient places to launch a kayak, sailboat, or motorboat. Oftentimes, they are adjacent to waterfront parks, expanding upon those assets. They are as varied as Seattle’s topography, and you can visit them any time.
Cycling is the best way to visit Seattle’s shoreline street ends. Many are accessed from low-traffic streets or bike paths.

Sitting beneath the Interstate 5 Ship Canal Bridge is the Furman Street street end. A fairly simple affair, it has a broad grass lawn leading to the water and a view towards the University of Washington campus and the several new highrises emerging in its neighborhood. Along Fuhrman and next to the street end is a rowing club, adding a nice buzz of activity.

WSDOT has closed the area off between the rowing club and the street end due to some hazards associated with falling debris from the underside of the bridge while it undergoes repairs. This condition will remain for some time until all necessary repairs are made. That being said it’s still worth a peek.

Partly sandy beach and partly forested landscape, the Martin Street street end can appear mysterious when viewed from Fairview Avenue due to its dense tree canopy and deep shadows. Probing beyond the shadows, however, one can find a waterfront bathed in sunlight. When I visited I happened upon a festive gathering that expanded my appreciation of street ends to be about more than water access and places to catch a view of the water to include unique social and gathering places. Residents from recent apartment development in the neighborhood have added new energy to what used to be a more isolated street end.
SDOT recently finished $375,000 in improvements (most done after these photos were taken). Even if you’ve previously visited the street end, here is a good reason to go again.

The most improved of Eastlake’s street ends, and among the most improved of those I have visited, is the East Allison Street street end. Although lacking the shelter and intimacy of East Martin Street, its staging area for watercraft, generous steps leading to the shoreline, and ADA accessible parking, make it very user friendly.
Right across from the street end is a new neighborhood corner coffee shop, adding a nice amenity to an otherwise desirable location.

East Hamlin Street combines many of the endearing features of Seattle’s street ends, albeit in rustic packaging. It provides a fantastic prospect for viewing Gas Works Park and an intimate lagoon with a sandy shoreline. Other amenities include park benches, a picnic table, as well as an ever changing assortment of lawn chairs along the waterline. The plantings include rose bushes, seagrasses, and a variety of other flora I’m ill equipped to identify. I especially liked the large deciduous trees hovering along its northern edge, their hues changing to golden in the fall day’s crisp air.

Things have been a little tidied up since I took these photos. The paths have new gravel and the benches were repaired, and the neighborhood stewards have done a great job improving and keeping the plantings looking great.

South of East Hamlin Street is East Edgar Street. Although not (yet) part of the Street End program, the Seattle Parks Foundation has information on potential improvements that you can learn more about.

Situated at the tail end of one of Eastlake’s few east-west arterials, Roanoke Street can be hard to miss despite its strategic location and generous amenities. If one looks beyond the parking area along its eastern edge, one finds new street furniture and a paved plaza.

Just to the north is a densely packed, and very urban collection of houseboats. Unlike other neighboring houseboat communities, those along Mallard Cove are arranged parallel to the shoreline giving them a density different from neighboring houseboat communities. This effect is further enhanced by the hillside buildings’ eastern edge.
Boeing’s first factory was located at the foot of Roanoke street.

Unique among the dozens of street ends I visited in the past, Louisa Street has a bocce court and a color theme, whose red brilliance was enhanced by the crimson trees hovering above its like-colored furniture when I visited in the fall.

Neighbors are calling it the Louisa Street Beach since children are having fun playing games in the sand. The two trees to the north have mulch and edging to keep users off the tree roots and we will do additional planting this Fall. This park gets lots of kayak use - a self-service rental is across the street. It also generally has someone simply sitting there and enjoying the day—in all kinds of weather.

Lynn Street Mini Park has a range of amenities and terrific views. Its sandy shoreline is a favorite launching spot for kayakers, and its generously furnished street level terrace allows one to glance above the water enthusiasts to Lake Union. Framed by houseboats to the south and a rare over the water condominium to the north, the park provides one of the more unique and beloved edges along the lake. Although not part of SDOT’s Street End program, and officially a Seattle City Park, its designation matters not for appreciating its fine qualities.

The East Boston Street street end is easily missed unless one has a map in hand. The street end itself is really just the sidewalk along Fairview Avenue – there is no access to the water. Instead, and if one picks just the right viewing angle to snatch a view between the heavily vegetated shoreline one is surprised to see a picturesque assembly of houseboats framing a view across the lake to Queen Anne.

East Newton Street, also known as Terry Pettus Park , is currently undergoing renovation. Prior to its being closed I was able to visit it on a fine fall day in 2023. This particular street end, at least prior to its renovation, had that rarest of amenities: a dock. The dock not only allows one a different way to access the water but it also provides a view back to the shoreline. It is hard to pick a favorite among the many great street ends along Eastlake Avenue, but Newton Street would certainly be a contender.
All construction permits for the renovation have been obtained and I’m sure the neighborhood eagerly awaits its reopening. Click here for project updates.

articles.title: Indigenous students retrace Lewis and Clark’s historic journey: ‘We can’t protect what we cannot see’
articles.author: Ashley Stimpson
paras: Two centuries after the expedition, Indigenous students are conducting a new wildlife survey along the route

In 1804, when Thomas Jefferson dispatched Meriwether Lewis and William Clark and their Corps of Discovery to explore the newly acquired land west of the Mississippi, the president’s primary aim was political: Americans needed to establish presence, power and trade routes in these territories before the Europeans beat them to it.

But Jefferson, an ardent naturalist, had a secondary agenda. He ordered that the expedition also survey the flora and fauna of these landscapes. On their two-year jaunt across the western half of the country, Lewis and Clark kept meticulous journals of the animals and plants they encountered: bison, horned lizards, sage grouse, prairie dogs, wild licorice and catfish, among them. These observations were pivotal in shaping an early understanding of North American biodiversity.

articles.title: The abortion doctor who leads with her faith: ‘God is forgiving’
articles.author: Melissa Hellmann with photographs by Idara Ekpoh
paras: Dr DeShawn Taylor runs Arizona’s only Black woman-owned abortion clinic amid rapid legal changes

When gynecologist and abortion provider Dr DeShawn Taylor has conversations with patients about the afterlife, they ask her if they will be condemned for their choices. To quell their concerns, she shares with them bible verses about free will. “If God wants that vessel, that spirit to get here, God will choose another vessel. You get to say, ‘I’ll pass,’” Taylor said at her clinic one spring afternoon, her short curly hair matching the color of her maroon scrubs. “I think that makes people feel a lot better with that understanding.”

As the founder and CEO of Desert Star Institute for Family Planning in Phoenix, Arizona, Taylor heads the only Black woman-run abortion clinic in the state, which also boasts a staff of women of color. On a Tuesday in March, pop music wafted throughout the waiting room filled mostly with Black and brown women, some with their children in tow. Bilingual posters about abortion care taped to the wall reflected the diversity of the clinic’s staff and clientele. On 6 February, an Arizona judge struck down state laws requiring patients to receive an ultrasound and to wait at least a day before receiving an abortion. With abortions now more accessible, a steady stream of clients poured into the office the week that the laws were repealed. By mid-March, appointments had petered out to a more manageable about 10 services a day.

articles.title: National ground stop response highlights critical errors in public reassurance – saying ‘nothing nefarious’ did the opposite of quelling public concern
articles.author:
<name>Shannon A. Bowen, Professor of Journalism and Mass Communications, University of South Carolina</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/shannon-a-bowen-766905"/>
paras: Thousands of travelers were stranded on Nov. 13, 2026, when the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all domestic flights in the U.S. because of what they said were failures in decades-old air traffic communications systems . Crisis communications expert Shannon A. Bowen , a scholar at the University of South Carolina’s College of Information and Communications, spoke with The Conversation’s Politics and Legal Affairs Editor, Naomi Schalit, about how the Trump administration handled the first day of the crisis.
Is there a first principle in crisis communications?

The first principle would be to react quickly and react with accuracy, react with everything you know at the moment, truthfully, but always react quickly. Because if you delay until you gather information, a vacuum will ensue. Information fills that vacuum that may not be accurate. And so that’s the enemy of accurate crisis communication, but you want to always speak quickly and be the most authoritative and definitive source, even if very little information is known.
What did we see on the day of the ground stop?

A crisis unfolded and to the administration’s credit, they did react very quickly , in a way that offered the information that was known at the time, even though not a lot was known about why the ground stop was issued until later.
You’re speaking about the short press conference that afternoon with Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin?

He did keep saying that nothing nefarious was at hand . And for a crisis communication scholar, you would not want to introduce the idea that something nefarious was at hand, unless, indeed, something nefarious was at hand. So by the very act of introducing this concept and this idea, I think the talking point, “Nothing nefarious,” then went across multiple networks, and it became the center of a controversy rather than quelling a controversy.

By saying nothing nefarious is at hand, that indeed confirmed something nefarious was at hand, even if the nefariousness was only the mismanagement of the air traffic control systems routers that they claimed caused the problem. By introducing this idea, I believe it did bring to mind that there may be other state actors behind whatever happened, that it could be a cyber attack. It would have been better to say, “We have evidence that this was not a cyber attack but a hardware failure.”
How did the later press conference with Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy go from your perspective as an expert on crisis communications?
They handled the questions that they received correctly. They told us as much information as they knew.
However, they did seem to downplay the extent of this crisis, because we have to remember the traveling public is not just people trying to get to business meetings.

We had football teams stranded. Now football Saturday , all over the SEC, has been disrupted. And there’s probably disruption in other areas of the country, but to us in the South, SEC football is almost a religious experience on Saturday . Luckily, the University of South Carolina football team had already flown out . But our marching band was stuck in this crisis, and so we have a lot of ripple effects from something like this happening, and it definitely says to me that this was an emergency situation. It wasn’t simply a crisis, it was an actual emergency of impending disaster-level scale.

If it were simply routers being overloaded, as we’ve been told, why wouldn’t they already know this situation and restart those routers the night before or over Friday night after most of the traveling public is out of the air?
What was Mullin’s and Duffy’s job when they got out there? What did they need to do?

To inform the public about the danger, why this happened, the extent of the problem, and what they’re doing to remediate the problem. We keep hearing that they’re asking for US$30 billion and more to repair the whole infrastructure for the air traffic control system, which is great, but what are they doing right now?

How do we know that flights in the air, right this minute, are any safer than the ones yesterday, a minute before the ground stop? Do we have that information? I don’t feel confident that they addressed that question appropriately. I don’t think that the traveling public entirely feels safe at this point or adequately informed that they will arrive at their destination.
They introduced politics into the press conference as well, didn’t they?

It’s something that they have the prerogative to do. They are both political appointees and members of the cabinet . So I understand that aspect, but I really wish they had addressed the traveling public’s concerns more overtly before making it political, that they need more money to fix this. We know they need more money to fix it, and I’m sure the American taxpayers are aware of the problem and willing to fund those corrections. But the more expedient issues would be, what about all these people who were stuck in airports ?
Were there warning signs for this crisis?

I believe there were. We had another ground stop about three years ago , due to air traffic control problems, and that is what we call in crisis communications a “prodrome ,” a warning sign of larger impending problems. When you see these types of warning signs, it really gives us a reason to think it’s going to get worse.

Duffy did say on Nov. 13 that, because of the condition of the air traffic infrastructure, “ you will have more ” ground stoppages. If you had a piece of advice for the administration regarding their future communications, what would you tell them?

I would say to communicate in advance as much as possible, so if you’re even considering a ground stop, it may be a good idea to put out a public notice so that people don’t go to the airport on a vacation flight, maybe they delay that for a week or two. It might also be a good idea to speak with the airline industry representatives and say, “Here’s what we’re thinking. Can you work with us? How can we make this better for the traveling public?” Also, if 17 of 22 routers were malfunctioning, could we have had a partial ground stop at only the affected airports, rather than a nationwide stop?
My silly last question: Do crisis communications experts have any theories about Friday the 13th?

We consider it more of a superstition, but I have noticed that there does tend to be a lot of activity on Friday the 13th. It might be placebo effect, it might be because we expect something bad to happen and we’re looking for it. But that day does seem to always have some type of activity. This is also when organizations release bad news, oftentimes, they say, “Let’s hold it until Friday the 13th, because bad news is expected.” People will assume, on Friday the 13th, that negative things are going to come out, so the shock value won’t be as much.
Shannon A. Bowen received funding in 2022-2023 from The National Science Foundation as PI on a grant studying disaster management.

articles.title: Officials blame aging FAA telecom gear as U.S. airspace reopens, see no link to Microsoft or AI
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Updated with officials’ explanation of the cause and the reopening of U.S. airspace.

The nationwide ground stop that halted U.S. commercial air travel Friday was not caused by the Microsoft 365 outage that began a day earlier, federal officials said at an evening news conference, blaming aging FAA telecom equipment that was overloaded with data.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened the news conference by raising the Microsoft outage himself. “I want to make sure everybody understands that there is no connection between this and Microsoft,” he said. “I know a lot of people are making that jump.”
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy likewise ruled out a role for SMART, the FAA’s new AI traffic-planning tool, saying it isn’t connected to the core systems controllers use to track flights.
“There was no possible way SMART would have impacted what happened today,” he said.

The FAA reopened U.S. airspace at 5:15 p.m. Pacific, more than four hours after the problems began, Duffy said. He said flights would resume slowly, depending on whether airlines had crews available, and some may not depart until Saturday morning.
Microsoft confirmed in a statement that it had no indication the FAA ground stop was related to its service disruption.

Asked whether a cyberattack or “rogue AI” could be ruled out, Mullin said there was “nothing completely certain right now,” but “it appears that this was mechanically driven.” He said he could not rule out the possibility of a cyberattack but said there was “zero evidence” of one so far.

What happened: Duffy said the FAA began seeing unstable radar and communications data at air traffic control facilities across the country at 12:36 p.m. Pacific. Aging switches and routers in the agency’s telecom network “got overloaded with data” and began producing inconsistent information, he said, adding that the FAA still relies on “1980s little copper lines.”
“Our new IP switches did not go down. It’s the old hardware that went down,” he said. The FAA restored service after deploying fixes to reduce the overloading on its switches, he said.

Mullin said the overload appeared to have been triggered by new equipment the FAA was installing. As the agency put “patches into the system” and added “new equipment and new technology,” he said, it “was overwhelming the older system.” Neither official said exactly what that equipment was.

The FAA is in the middle of replacing its legacy telecom network with a modern internet-protocol network. AT&T took over the lead role on that project in August with an initial $74.3 million award, as the FAA works toward a goal of finishing by the end of 2028.
Duffy and Mullin used the briefing to press Congress for money to finish rebuilding the air traffic control system. Mullin said President Trump has declared the situation a national emergency.
The administration has asked Congress for an additional $30.1 billion for aviation infrastructure, AeroTime reported . Duffy said at the evening news conference that he wants $50 billion.

Earlier in the day, Mullin had said officials were looking into a possible link to SMART, including through DHS’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). The FAA said Tuesday it was expanding the system to the airspace managed by all 22 of its en route air traffic control centers.

The agency describes SMART as a cloud-based system that pulls in about 200 data streams, including weather, flight paths and controller staffing, to recommend flight schedules and routes. FAA specialists review its recommendations, and local facilities decide whether to act on them.

SMART is part of a 12-year, $875 million FAA contract with Boston-based Air Space Intelligence, which denied any connection to the issue. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said.

The FAA halted departures nationwide shortly before 1 p.m. Pacific. More than 3,500 planes were in the air at the time, Duffy said. It’s the second nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11 attacks, after a January 2023 failure of the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions system.
FlightAware counted nearly 7,000 flights delayed or canceled as of Friday afternoon.

articles.title: Blue Origin puts its space station plans on hold to concentrate on moon missions instead
articles.author: Alan Boyle
paras: Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin space venture has decided not to seek further NASA funding for its Orbital Reef space station project in order to tighten its focus on lunar missions.

For the past five years, Blue Origin has played a lead role in Orbital Reef , alongside partners including Sierra Space and Boeing. In late 2021, Blue Origin won a $130 million contract from NASA in the first phase of the space agency’s Commercial Low Earth Orbit Destinations program, or CLD.

Now NASA is seeking proposals for the next phase of the program , which will fund the development of orbital outposts to replace International Space Station in the 2030s. Proposals are due on Dec. 8, with contracts expected to be awarded next spring.
Blue Origin indicated that it will not submit a bid.

“Blue Origin’s mission is to build a road to space for the benefit of Earth so that millions of people can live and work in space. Establishing a sustained human presence on the moon is a critical step toward that future,” the company said in an emailed statement.

“As our role supporting NASA’s Artemis and Moon Base missions continues to grow, we’re focusing resources on capabilities that directly advance our lunar projects,” Blue Origin said. “By sharpening that focus, we can move faster on the technologies and infrastructure needed to make lunar permanence a reality.”

Orbital Reef was once touted as a “mixed-use business park” in space — and was even slated to star in a sci-fi thriller titled “Helios.” But much like that delayed film project, the space station is now on the back burner.

Orbital Reef isn’t the only initiative Blue Origin has put on hold to prioritize moon missions. In January, the company suspended its suborbital New Shepard program for at least two years for similar reasons.

Blue Origin is building landers for delivering cargo and crews to the lunar surface for NASA. An uncrewed Blue Moon Mark 1 lunar lander is scheduled for launch early next year, and a crew-capable Mark 2 version is scheduled for testing in low Earth orbit next year during NASA’s Artemis 3 mission.

Last week , NASA awarded Blue Origin a $94 million base contract, plus a $140 million option, to deliver a nuclear-powered rover to the lunar south pole. Blue Origin also won a spot in NASA’s broader lunar cargo delivery program. In addition, Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin subsidiary, will contribute to a lunar power-generating project known as miniCAST.
Blue Origin is pursuing several other moon development initiatives, including a program called Blue Alchemist that aims to use lunar materials to manufacture solar cells and electrical wire.

Several competitors are still working on commercial space stations. Voyager Technologies, Airbus and Northrop Grumman lead the Starlab consortium, which received CLD Phase 1 funding from NASA and is expected to put in a proposal for Phase 2.

Axiom Space and Vast are also developing outposts that could take the place of the ISS. Meanwhile, Marysville, Wash.-based Gravitics is building space station hardware for Axiom and an orbital carrier for the U.S. Space Force .

articles.title: Araceli raises $4.5M for drug discovery tools aimed at reducing animal testing
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Araceli Biosciences , a Portland-area biotech company, has secured $4.5 million in funding to help commercialize technology and develop new products that support using human cells instead of animal studies to test new drugs.

The Tigard, Ore., startup offers instruments and software for creating images of cells and automating analysis. Its technologies fall under the umbrella term “New Approach Methodologies,” which includes human-tissue models, computer simulations and AI-based approaches that reduce or avoid experimentation on animals such as mice, rats and monkeys.

Supporters of the methods, known as NAMs, argue that they can yield better outcomes because animals are not a perfect substitute for humans and can generate irrelevant findings. That can lead to costly, time-intensive development of drugs that fail to perform in people. Advocates also promote the alternatives as more humane.
The National Institutes of Health announced $84 million in September to build infrastructure for NAMs research at 10 sites nationwide.

“[T]he efforts signal a significant investment into human-based technologies as the future of preclinical science, aiming to make research faster, more predictive, and more directly relevant to human health,” the NIH said in a release .

Araceli said it has raised a total of $22.7 million from investors. The new round was led by William Cortelyou and included Fluke Venture Partners, according to PitchBook. The company disclosed Thursday that businessman and animal welfare advocate Jeff Swickard was also an investor.
Swickard owns 54 auto dealerships across Western states and is a commercial real estate investor with $250 million invested in Portland properties.
Shawn MacDonald, chief financial officer for Araceli, said Swickard’s “support reflects a belief that we share, which is that better science and more humane science go hand-in-hand.”
Araceli launched in 2023 as a spinoff from Phoseon Technology, which makes UV LED units for industrial curing and life sciences applications.

The company said that companies and institutions using Araceli technology include the Max Planck Institute and Evotec in Germany, the Wertheim UF Scripps Institute in Florida, VALID Therapeutics in Boston, and Ginkgo Bioworks, as well as large pharmaceutical companies. It has 30 employees.

articles.title: Shoreline Pedestrian Bridge Defect Jeopardizes Already Delayed Timeline
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Any remaining hope of Shoreline opening its new pedestrian bridge over I-5 this winter appear dashed, after the project ran into a snag this month. KIRO reporter Chris Sullivan broke the news on Tuesday, noting builders were delaying the bridge placement that had been slated for November.

“Unfortunately, the contractor has discovered some manufacturing issues with one of the arches,” a City spokesperson told KIRO . “They are currently working with the manufacturer to resolve the issue. At this point, it is unclear if the manufacturer will be able to make corrections on site with the existing arch or if they will have to make a whole new arch. It will be another couple of weeks before they know for sure, and we have a new timeline.”

While Shoreline and its contractor, Kraemer North America, are still determining the extent of the issue, the City is framing it as a minor setback, with a spring 2027 opening still feasible. In fact, the City's project website portrays a spring 2027 opening as essentially the plan all along.

However, that would represent a significant delay from initial plans. In 2020, The Urbanist reported Shoreline was still hoping to open the pedestrian bridge close to concurrently with the light rail station. Lining up funding added planning delays, but an early 2026 opening had still been targeted once the project's $40 million budget had been assembled in 2024 , as Urbanist coverage noted at the time.

"While the project was in design we developed an early 2026 opening estimate. Securing final approvals to advertise for construction bids took longer than we anticipated, delaying that step by several months," Shoreline spokesperson Tavia Tan told The Urbanis t. "We advertised for bids in December 2024. Once the contractor joined the project, we updated the schedule based on the bridge manufacturer’s production timeline and input from the construction team. Those factors led to an estimate of 'early 2027' for the full bridge opening. Earlier this fall, we revised that projection to spring of 2027, primarily due to delays in procuring materials. This revision occurred before we identified the manufacturing issue."

Shoreline's two light rail stations opened on August 30, 2024, along with the rest of the Lynnwood Link extension . While the City had hoped to open the bridge as close to possible as light rail's arrival, it could end up being close to three years after the fact.

Once the pedestrian bridge is in place, residents in the rapidly densifying neighborhood to the west of I-5, which Shoreline rezoned in 2016 , will have direct access to South Shoreline Station without having to head down to the busy overpass at 145th Street – a street that is being supercharged with highway-style roundabouts.

If plans to place the bridge span this month had gone forward, the project still had other hurdles to clear before it could have opened, including completing a direct ramp to the light rail station platform and a trail connection on the west side linking people walking, rolling, and biking to 1st Avenue NE, a corridor which has been among the focal points of midrise development in the area.
The contractor plans to move forward with the trail work while the bridge span issue is being rectified.

"The original construction schedule called for placing the bridge span before building the connecting trail to 1st Avenue NE," Tan said. "The contractor has rearranged the work and is now building the trail. This flexibility allows construction to continue and helps limit delays while we determine the next steps for the bridge."

Sullivan noted a brief night-time freeway closure will be necessary once the bridge span is ready for installation: "You have likely seen the massive structure being built along the west side of the freeway for months. Shoreline had targeted Saturday, Nov. 7, or Saturday, Nov. 14, as the nights to close I-5 and lift the bridge into place. That installation has been delayed, but other work on the project is continuing."

Despite the lack of a pedestrian bridge, both of Shoreline's stations have been success stories, generating robust homebuilding activity and solid initial ridership numbers . Shoreline South averaged more than 3,600 daily boardings in October, boosted by a bus restructure that truncated Sound Transit's Route 522 bus at the station.

Shoreline North hovered around 2,800 daily boardings in September and October. Overall, the 1 Line corridor amassed just over 155,000 daily boardings in October, making it the busiest light rail system in the United States.
The addition of Shoreline's pedestrian bridge and continued residential growth offer a potent combination to build on that momentum.

articles.title: Five More Washington Cities Selected for State Growth Plan Reviews in 2027
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Washington's Commerce Department has released a list of five cities and towns that will see their housing growth plans subjected to additional state scrutiny next year, the second set of reviews planned under the 2025 Housing Accountability Act . Burlington, Friday Harbor, Mount Vernon, Oak Harbor, and Washougal will go under the microscope, with city leaders given deadlines to make any updates to their local Comprehensive Plans with the goal of ensuring that development regulations intended to pave the way for more diverse housing types across a range of income levels are in place.

The 2027 cities are mostly clustered around the north end of Puget Sound, in counties that had a state-mandated December 31, 2025 deadline to overhaul their local Comprehensive Plans. All five cities faced that deadline and didn't meet it, either leaving Commerce out of the loop when it comes to updating their plan or submitting a draft plan that the state found to fall short in some way.

The Housing Accountability Act represents something of a sea change in local housing growth planning that cities are still getting used to. Prior to its implementation, the only way to challenge a Comprehensive Plan that looked to be out-of-compliance with state law was to file a challenge at the state's Growth Management Hearings Board, a case-by-case appeal process that usually fell on private groups like neighborhood organizations or the statewide land use advocacy non-profit Futurewise to pursue.

Though the Commerce Department is often tasked with providing recommendations on local development standards and zoning changes, there wasn't a mechanism available to hold cities and towns that went too far their own way accountable. With the Housing Accountability Act, cities and towns are given a compliance deadline to make essential changes and if those aren't enacted, the so-called Builder's Remedy goes into effect – with local permit departments unable to deny building permits for residential projects that meet certain affordability requirements, regardless of the underlying zoning. Theoretically, that could mean skyscrapers in areas of the city that aren't used to dense housing.

Commerce is still in the middle of its 2026 "selected review" process, with zoning changes already adopted in three of the eight jurisdictions that made the list this year. So far, only Carnation has gotten to the stage of approving a final plan that is still being reviewed by Commerce, with Bainbridge Island and the 300-resident town of Beaux Arts Village both adopting interim regulations that provide additional time to adopt permanent changes down the road.

Next week, the City of DuPont, tucked into South Pierce County near Joint Base Lewis-McChord, is poised to be the first city to actually trigger the Builder's Remedy. Despite a timeline that doesn't call for adoption of potential changes to the city's Comprehensive Plan until early next year, DuPont has not requested an extension from Commerce that would prevent the Builder's Remedy from taking effect.

Though many of the jurisdictions that have been subjected to review so far have been relatively small, the impact is adding up. By the end of the second year, Commerce is on track to have reviewed cities and towns accounting for approximately 144,000 residents, more people than live in Washington's sixth largest city of Kent.

In turning its attention to Friday Harbor, Commerce will be jumping into the fray when it comes to one of the state's thorniest housing crises. As a tourist-oriented city with a high rate of seasonal housing, housing in Friday Harbor is regularly out-of-reach of the workers that the local economy relies on. Housing prices within San Juan County rose more than 100% between 2016 and 2022, far faster than median wages could ever compete with.

Despite increased demand for units in Friday Harbor, projects proposed in the city often turn highly contentious. Last year, a 49-unit development near Friday Harbor elementary school drew significant opposition, despite the inclusion of eight units of workforce housing in the project. The concerns raised included increased traffic, traffic safety impacts, and a lack of overall infrastructure, but the common denominator was the idea that Friday Harbor can't handle more population density.

Amanda Lynn, Executive Director of the San Juan Community Home Trust, offered an overall view of housing growth on San Juan Island, in an interview with the The Journal of the San Juans about that specific project.

“Every time you add a housing unit on this island, that requires infrastructure, that requires community resources like fire, police, school, anything you can think of,” Lynn said. “Every housing unit requires these things. So there’s always a balance beyond even just thinking about the ecosystem balance of the island itself.”
That balancing act, while clearly necessary in some regard on a ferry-dependent island, often means that lower-income residents trying to find homes in San Juan Island get the short end of the stick.

A state review under the Housing Accountability Act won't be able to fully solve Friday Harbor's housing crisis, of course. But it will likely ensure that barriers that stand in the way of housing production that aren't aligned with state law don't stay in place, adding clear repercussions if they do.

As these reviews continue to ramp up, pushback from local elected officials is another thing to watch for. As Beaux Arts Village councilmembers took their vote on interim development regulations last month, they also vowed to push for legislative changes that would modify the Housing Accountability Act to be less impactful on them. So far, what exactly it would look like to water down the legislation hasn't become clear, but as larger cities start to get subjected to that review, the political pressure could ramp up.

For now, however, the Housing Accountability Act does appear to be having its intended impact, slowly bringing along jurisdictions that otherwise would be lagging when it comes to legalizing housing, one by one.

articles.title: Nailed it: Muse Crush expanding to Capitol Hill with ‘almost overwhelming’ selection of press-on nails
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: “The first and only handmade press-on nail store in Seattle” is expanding to Capitol Hill.
Muse Crush is bringing its crafted and unique press-on nail sets and collectibles to E Pike. The shop’s signature pink paint job is already complete.

Seattle entrepreneur Jinger Zhao founded the business online in 2022 before opening a storefront on NE 43rd in the U-District. An “amazing, gorgeous, almost overwhelming selection,” one review from a shopper reads.

The press-on nail boutique and “Japanese-inspired kawaii cute, and creative gift shop” will replace Capitol Hill’s only self-serve kombucha taproom. Portland-born SOMA Kombucha shuttered its taps following a late 2025 run-in with a SUV that smashed into the storefront.

Muse Crush Capitol Hill will soon neighbor Sal’s Barbershop and HoneyHole just down the block from Doghouse Leathers and Babeland at the corner of E Pike and Boylston. Just look for Mina, the giant blue lounging cat in the mural around the corner from the newly-painted-pink storefront.

Unlike mass-produced drugstore strips, Muse Crush’s nail sets are handmade with hand-painted artwork including creations from local artists, plus sculpted finishes, and 3D charms, and are sold in sizes from extra-small to large across short and long lengths. Priced around $28 to $30, each set includes adhesive tabs, a nail file, and a wooden cuticle stick.
Beyond nails, the shop stocks blind-box figurines, plush keychains, jewelry, stickers, and goods from local creators.
Muse Crush will open soon at 701 E Pike. Learn more at musecrush.co .

articles.title: Medical examiner: Man found behind Capitol Hill grocery store died of overdose
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: The King County Medical Examiner says a man found dead behind the Capitol Hill Safeway Monday morning died of a drug overdose.

Seattle Police and Seattle Fire were called to the E Thomas side of the grocery just after 11:30 AM to a report of a man down and blood at the scene. Responders closed off the area and medical investigators were called in.
According to the examiner, Elijah J. Coolshaun Goodall died of acute combined drug intoxication including fentanyl and methamphetamine in an accidental overdose. The Seattle man was 35.

articles.title: Wilson’s veto stands as Seattle City Council tussles over flipped vote
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Mayor Katie Wilson’s veto of Seattle City Council legislation to create a parking permit system for people living homeless in RVs will stand.
The council voted 5–4 on Thursday to sustain the veto falling a vote short of the majority needed to enact street parking limits and the permitting system for RVs.
District 3 Councilmember and Council President Joy Hollingsworth voted to override the veto, joining Councilmembers Debora Juarez, Bob Kettle, Maritza Rivera, and bill sponsor Dan Strauss .

Ahead of the vote, residents, service providers, and business representatives weighed in during a packed hybrid public comment session limited to one-minute addresses per speaker. The majority urged the council to uphold the veto, contending that Seattle lacks sufficient safe parking lots and shelter beds. Outreach workers and unhoused residents warned that tying permits to a rigid, one-time census would lead to towed and impounded homes.

Speaking to conditions in District 3, one commenter who works with unhoused individuals in Cal Anderson Park argued against banning RVs as a form of “collective punishment” when residents already face severe instability.
Business leaders from Ballard and North Seattle urged an override to curb illegal drug markets and neighborhood blight.

Wilson has matched her veto with an executive order focused on immediate service deployment rather than administrative permitting. The order directs city departments to immediately release 2026 outreach funding, fast-track the opening and occupancy of two RV safe lots designed to accommodate 182 residents, and establish a cross-departmental and community working group to troubleshoot right-of-way conditions and address neighborhood impacts using existing laws.

During debate Thursday, Hollingsworth rejected claims that the legislation passed by the council and vetoed by Wilson was punitive, arguing that preserving the status quo fails both vehicle residents and frustrated neighbors. Pointing to the city’s $228 million homelessness budget and calling the King County Regional Homeless Authority’s execution a “complete disaster,” she demanded accountability and tangible results.
“It might make us feel good about allocating millions of dollars, but without outcomes, now that is cruel and inhumane,” Hollingsworth said.

With progressive-leaning Councilmembers Alexis Mercedes Rinck, Eddie Lin, and Dionne Foster voting no, West Seattle’s Rob Saka represented a key swing vote, joining the “no” side against overturning the veto after previously voting for the original bill.

Saka praised sponsor Strauss for a “herculean effort” on the legislative package while explaining his own decision to flip his vote and sustain the mayor’s veto. Saka framed his shift as exercising the “humility and grace to change your mind” to give the mayor’s executive order a fair shot — emphasizing human dignity, a “carrot and stick” balance of compassion and accountability, and geographic equity for his heavily impacted District 1.

Tensions flared during closing remarks when Strauss argued that the mayor’s 60-day task force could easily run concurrently with his bill’s built-in review period, characterizing the argument that sustaining the veto represented a “new path” as “duplicitous” and a vote for the status quo.

Following a point of order raised by Lin over council rules against impugning colleagues’ motives, a visibly frustrated Saka scolded Strauss for “Seattle passive aggressive, subtle slights,” challenging him to take any grievances up directly in their adjacent offices rather than questioning his character or integrity. Strauss maintained that he was merely pointing out a factual overlap in policy timelines rather than attacking Saka’s motives.

The RV debate comes as the council is winding up final changes to the mayor’s 2027-2028 budget plan including tapping $31 million in JumpStart payroll tax reserves and cutting $22 million in pension transfers to reverse cuts proposed by Wilson to address a looming budget deficit.

It also arrives as the Wilson administration is shifting its strategies around homelessness including expanded timelines for reaching shelter goals and changes in how encampment removals are prioritized as parks like Cal Anderson generate more than 1,000 citizen complaints about illegal encampments per year.
With the veto holding, attention now shifts to Wilson’s executive order to expand outreach and safe parking alternatives.

articles.title: Three reported robbed at gunpoint in Seattle Central parking garage hold-up
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: See something others should know about? Email CHS or call/txt (206) 399-5959 . You can view recent CHS 911 coverage here. Hear sirens and wondering what’s going on? Check out reports from @jseattle or join and check in with neighbors in the CHS Facebook Group .
A group was robbed at gunpoint on the third floor of the Seattle Central parking garage early last Saturday.

The victims told police the suspect had fled in a vehicle.

The robbery has not been included in the Seattle Police Department’s Significant Incident Reports updates for the East Precinct and came to light through CHS’s routine review of SPD dispatch data. CHS reported here on the changing nature of public information provided by the East Precinct.

articles.title: The Stranger’s Noise Complaint: XOË
articles.author: Stranger Staff
paras: Welcome to Noise Complaint, The Stranger ‘s new audio and video music podcast featuring live performances right here at The Stranger HQ. Streamed live and released every other Friday, we invite a great band, musician, or wonderfully weird act to perform. Tune in, discover something new, and support art in your city.

The output of XOË—Zoë Duarte (vocals), Max Irvine (keyboards, guitar), Saba Samakar (drums), Adrian Michael (bass, guitar, drums)—is small so far, but it instantly ensnares you in its charms. Capturing a big chunk of your attention is the slyly seductive grain of Duarte’s voice, which, incidentally, is summarized by the title of their fantastic song “Sweet Sensation.” XOË (pronounced “X-O-E”) really blossom on their most recent release, the stellar Blur of a Dream EP; the slow-motion whirlpool of “Feed Me” is as dankly alluring as early Tricky. The earlier track “Nighttime Blues” bears the erotic mesmerism as Scritti Politti’s “The ’Sweetest Girl.’” Boudoir-friendly R&B may be the band’s dominant mode, but Irvine’s capable of florid keyboard arabesques worthy of jazz legends George Duke and Chick Corea. articles.title: SIFF Cinema Workers Union Say Management Has ‘Unilaterally Suspended’ Bargaining
articles.author: Chase Hutchinson
paras: It’s been a great year for independent movie theaters in Seattle. But not for the workers in the SIFF Cinema Workers Union (SCWU). For the majority of 2026, they’ve been operating without a contract and bargaining has been slow going. Now, they say it’s been brought to a standstill. On top of that, SCWU claims management has retaliated against a union member, a charge SIFF disputes.
SCWU has filed an unfair labor practice (ULP) with the National Labor Relations Board—their second this year—over these issues and say they are now “actively discussing next steps.”

In a statement, the union said SIFF “unilaterally suspended the bargaining process” and “no progress has been made since the summer.” Back then, members expressed cautious optimism that SIFF was bargaining fairly after union members walked out before sold-out 70mm screenings of The Odyssey at SIFF Cinema Downtown. After providing management with a proposal in late August on the remaining issues in their contract and giving SIFF “extra time” to return to the union with a counterproposal, SIFF hasn’t been forthcoming at the subsequent meetings. They now say that SIFF abruptly canceled a meeting scheduled earlier last month “hours before it was meant to start” and haven’t scheduled any additional bargaining meetings since.

In response to a request for a comment and questions about the current state of contract negotiations, a spokesperson for SIFF said “there are next steps in the process but that is a conversation between the SCWU and SIFF, so we have no further comment at this time.” Previously, the organization said that it was “committed to good faith bargaining,” pointing to the number of bargaining sessions they’d taken part in (21 as of August) over the past several months as a demonstration of this commitment.

In regards to the ULP, the spokesperson said “SIFF welcomes the NLRB review of the ULP complaint as we are confident that they will find it baseless.” Asked where this confidence comes from and if they were similarly confident about the first ULP, which the NLRB has yet to rule on, the spokesperson declined to comment.

The union alleges that, in addition to outstanding concerns around transparency and what they say is “SIFF’s outright refusal to respond to a request for information regarding budgetary data,” management has retaliated against a member of union leadership.

“They gave this individual a ‘final warning’ within one disciplinary meeting, which violates the disciplinary rules set up in the contract,” Nico Hall, a SCWU member and member of the bargaining team, says. “The contract requires SIFF to gradually move an employee up several stages of discipline. Instead, SIFF has skipped through this process and placed this employee’s livelihood at risk.”

In response to the specific allegation of retaliation, a spokesperson for SIFF said they don’t “comment on any personnel matters,” but said that the organization “follows all internal processes as delineated in our employee handbook as well as the processes laid out in the agreement with the Union” and that “SIFF has not taken retaliatory action against any employee.”

Previously, the union has stopped short of calling for a boycott of SIFF or any of their theaters, which include SIFF Cinema Downtown, the SIFF Cinema Uptown, and SIFF Film Center. So far, they still aren’t calling for a boycott, but they won’t stop anyone who feels like boycotting.

“If SIFF customers feel motivated to boycott SIFF in response to their egregious mishandling of the bargaining process, SCWU would appreciate that support, especially if said customers send a message to SIFF warning them that their actions are losing business for the organization,” SCWU said in a statement.

articles.title: Katie Wilson’s RV Ban Veto Survives!
articles.author: Guy Oron
paras: On Thursday, the Seattle City Council officially declined to override Mayor Katie Wilson’s veto , killing the effective RV ban it passed last month. Bill sponsor Dan Strauss, who was very upset about the whole thing, garnered only five votes for the override, failing to meet the two-thirds threshold he needed to override a mayoral veto.

Everyone saw this coming after Councilmember Rob Saka’s last-minute change of position on the ordinance last week. It puts an end to a bruising political fight between Wilson and Strauss, who is also the council’s budget chair.

The vote ensures hundreds of homeless Seattleites who live in RVs and other large vehicles won’t have to enroll in a specialized permitting system to retain the right to park for 72 hours on city streets. Advocates said the proposed system—which would have only allowed people surveyed in a one-time census to obtain a permit— wouldn’t work for most RV residents who are transient and may lack other forms of paperwork.

Wilson issued the veto against the bill— her first as mayor— because the permitting system would be difficult to enforce, legally risky, expensive (costing about $3.5 million over the next five years), and could drive more people into unsheltered homelessness. The city charter required the council to vote on Wilson’s veto within 30 days.

Despite losing the veto vote, Strauss succeeded in passing most of his legislative agenda on RV resident reforms, including four ordinances and one non-binding resolution. These changes include adding more funding for vehicle resident outreach, authorizing city-owned vehicle storage lots, and updating the city’s definition of “junk vehicles” to streamline parking enforcement. Strauss’s proposal for a working group was also incorporated in Wilson’s executive order signed last week. An interim report is due in early January, with final recommendations expected by the end of March.

Wilson’s veto came after fierce opposition from homeless service providers, vehicle residents, and other progressive advocates. Alison Eisinger, executive director of the Seattle/King County Coalition on Homelessness, says that as of yesterday, constituents had sent more than 4,700 emails to council members and the mayor. About 30 people testified at yesterday’s special meeting, with most speaking against the RV ban.

Prior to the vote, council members spent about an hour relitigating their perspectives on the legislation. Strauss stubbornly defended his bill, saying “doing nothing is not an option.” He also compared advocates’ concerns about the “harmful” and “draconian” nature of the permitting system to the type of complaints middle-class neighbors tend to lodge against new shelter and affordable housing.

“These are the same concerns of complexity, of expense, of potential harmful impacts that I have literally heard about setting up tiny house villages [and] providing medically assisted treatment at shelters,” Strauss said.

Other moderates on the council reiterated their positions. Councilmember Bob Kettle said the impacts on neighborhoods by RV residents needed to be considered; Councilmembers Maritza Rivera and Debora Juarez said drug dealing, sex trafficking, and other crimes were being committed in RVs. Juarez, an interim appointee who will be replaced by newly elected progressive Nilu Jenks in two weeks, also had choice words for Wilson’s leadership, saying the public would see her veto as “dishonesty, inconsistency, [and] lack of leadership.”

The three progressives on the council, while (thankfully) less verbose, also stuck to their same talking points before the vote. Councilmember Dionne Foster said the one-time nature of the permitting system was a deal breaker, as it would exclude future families who may become homeless and have to live in their vehicles. Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck thanked advocates for their testimony, while Councilmember Eddie Lin called for unity despite policy disagreements.
Saka, whose pivotal flip-flop changed the outcome of the vote, said leadership is in part about “having the humility and grace to change your mind if new information becomes available.”

His comments seemed to anger Strauss, who responded that calling the mayor’s veto “‘a new path’ is duplicitous.” In a point of order, Saka accused Strauss of impugning his motives, motivation, and character, which is against the council’s decorum rules. What’s a council meeting without a little drama, right?
Strauss’s comments angered activists, too. Chanel Horner, a human rights advocate and former vehicle resident who currently lives in a tiny home, saw it as a false equivalence.
“He tried to compare us to Republicans, and that was unfounded,” Horner said. “Republicans are like ‘not in my backyard.’ We’re basically the opposite.”

Eisinger also took issue with the stigmatizing framing of RV residents as a public safety issue; instead of going through the council’s human services committee, Strauss’s bill was passed by the public safety committee. She says serious crime should be investigated and dealt with regardless of if the perpetrator lives in a house or a vehicle.

Now that Strauss’s bill is dead, where will the money for establishing the permitting program go? Strauss sponsored a budget provision to prevent Wilson from spending the roughly $800,000 a year on other purposes. He wants the RV working group to release its recommendations before unlocking those funds, which will require another vote by the city council.

Here’s an idea: Services and shelter for homeless vehicle residents are woefully underfunded. After a year and a half without any safe lots in the city, the Low Income Housing Institute is set to open Glassyard Commons in West Seattle later this month, which will have 72 spots available.

The city is setting aside funding for a second safe lot to open next year, which Horner argued should go to a different service provider so that homeless people have multiple options to choose from. But even that won’t be enough, she says, and ultimately there just isn’t enough housing available for everyone living on the streets.
“If we just had more housing, we’d have somewhere to move people to,” Horner said. “We wouldn’t have to be in an RV in the first place.”

articles.title: Seattle’s Leaders are Notably Absent from Nationwide Boycott of Starbucks Over Labor Abuses
articles.author: Hunter Pauli
paras: After years of organizing and prolonged contract negotiations over better working conditions, Starbucks Workers United (SBWU) union members announced a nationwide boycott campaign in late August calling on allies to force the fast food company to the negotiating table.

Starbucks workers rallied at 40 college campuses nationwide yesterday, including the University of Washington, calling on administrators to put ties with the coffee chain over its labor abuses. Seattle City Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck spoke at the UW rally in support of the boycott and urged the university to kick Starbucks off campus.

Politicians across the country are joining the boycott, including seven sitting congressmen and six new ones, as well as two US senators (none of these are local) and city councils across the country. Several state-level Democratic parties, including Washington’s, are part of the boycott, according to a recent count.
But here in Seattle, where the company was founded and remains based, the political class isn’t so quick to join.
Among local politicians, King County Councilmember Teresa Mosqueda and Washington House Rep. Shaun Scott have publicly joined the boycott, though it’s not exactly a big club.
But the most notable absent voice is Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson.

Among Wilson’s first acts after being elected mayor was to announce at an SBWU strike rally that she was boycotting Starbucks and that others should too. Notably there was no active nationwide boycott campaign called by SBWU when Wilson said “I am not buying Starbucks, and you should not either,” last November.

Over the next six months, Wilson was smeared by conservative media for advocating a boycott of a local corporation over its poor labor record. This included a column in the Wall Street Journal ‘s notoriously right-wing editorial pages written by former Starbucks owner Howard Schultz.

“Seattle’s mayor, Katie Wilson, has chosen to cast business as a foil rather than a partner. Her socialist rhetoric vilifies employers, even while she continues to rely on them for revenue,” Schultz wrote.

The attacks on Wilson are consistent with an ongoing campaign by business leaders opposing progressive taxation of Seattle’s corporate titans, who have spun a narrative of growing capital flight to the libertarian climates of the former Confederacy.

Wilson denounced her own prior support for a Starbucks boycott to the New York Times in May of this year, calling her words “not productive in the sense that they caused more harm than good,” and saying she wants “a multidimensional relationship” with local corporations.

“Multidimensional” is an accurate self-assessment, as the Mayor’s Office has, in recent months, assumed a quantum superposition of pledging to support unionization efforts at Starbucks while simultaneously walking back Wilson’s prior support for a boycott, a tactic Starbucks workers are now using to pressure the company.

In a FOX 13 interview broadcast June 3, Wilson told the interviewer “I guess I broke my boycott” by ordering a blueberry muffin latte during a visit to Starbucks’ Pike Place Market location when she went to the store “to talk to the workers there who are organizing a union.”
Since ending her spontaneous boycott this summer, SBWU announced their official nationwide boycott campaign, and the mayor’s nebulous position on the matter has only become more unclear.

At a recent press conference, Wilson refused to answer a direct question from The Stranger as to whether she was or was not boycotting Starbucks in light of the union’s new boycott campaign and her prior support.

“I absolutely support Starbucks workers’ right to organize and to join a union, and I want to see the union and the company bargaining in good faith and getting to a fair contract,” she said, declining to answer the question again when pressed.
Asked when she last went to Starbucks, Wilson said she did not remember.

Despite the hedging, giving no response when asked if she’s boycotting Starbucks effectively means the mayor is sticking with her prior decision to end her boycott, even if saying so publicly has now been made politically unfeasible by SBWU’s formal boycott campaign.

SBWU isn’t rushing to throw Wilson under the bus however, or, at least, leadership isn’t. Asked for comment on the mayor’s recent cryptic statements, SBWU told The Stranger “Mayor Katie Wilson has long stood shoulder-to-shoulder with union baristas, including on the picket line, and we’re proud to have her support in our fight for a fair contract.”

The statement continued: “Our union movement has taken the nation by storm, and the Starbucks boycott continues to grow in strength as elected officials, state parties, unions and consumers nationwide put their weight behind us and show their commitment to working people everywhere. Together, we will continue to fight for a fair contract that addresses systemic challenges like understaffing, low pay, unpredictable hours and more.”

While she is a self-proclaimed socialist, Wilson’s summertime reneging on her Starbucks boycott exemplifies that she is not a product of the labor movement, the traditional incubator of socialist politics. On October 1, the Washington State Labor Council announced the powerful state union federation was joining the boycott until baristas win a fair contract. Other major labor groups joining the boycott include the AFL-CIO and SEIU.

Until the union’s demands are met, SBWU is calling on boycotters to “run a Starbucks-free organization,” not contract with the company, encourage others to join, and “show up and show out to help union baristas win a fair contract.”
